Power · Ghana

Structures inside your transmission right of way, mapped and measured

Ghana’s transmission-line protection regulations set protected distances either side of 161 kV and 330 kV lines. AfriScan measures each structure’s distance from the centre line, groups the results along the line, and shows your land-management team where the corridor is filling up, so safety, engagement and compensation planning start from the same dated facts. A person reviews the results before they reach you.

Send your line route See sample outputs

The problem, in your words

Under the line, and around the towers

A transmission line crosses farmland, forest, towns and market centres. The strip beneath it changes between line inspections, and every change is a safety question first.

“Structures keep going up under the line.”

Kiosks, sheds, workshops, walls and houses appear inside the protected strip, most often where a line crosses a town or runs beside a busy road. Each one is easier to plan for while it is new and few.

“Someone has dug close to a tower.”

Fresh excavation, spoil and trenching near tower bases and inside the strip show at the surface. We flag them between surveys so line teams know which towers to visit first.

“The corridor is growing back.”

Vegetation regrows between clearing cycles, and bush fires can reach the line. Both show on dated imagery, stretch by stretch.

“We need facts before we talk to the community.”

Engagement with chiefs, assemblies and the people along the line goes better when everyone looks at the same dated map of what stands where.

The protected strips

What the transmission-line protection regulations set

A summary of the public rules as of 27 September 2026, for orientation. It is not legal advice; the sources are linked.

The Volta River Authority (Transmission Line Protection) Regulations 1967 (L.I. 542, Gazette of 5 May 1967), made under the Volta River Development Act 1961 (Act 46) and amended by the (Amendment) Regulations 2004 (L.I. 1737, Gazette of 20 February 2004), protect the land along high-voltage lines.

As GRIDCo, the national transmission company, described them in September 2026, they prohibit “drilling, excavation, lorry parks, shops, garages, barns and real estate development within a distance of 15 metres on either side of the centre of 161-kilovolt (kV) transmission lines and 20 metres for 330kV lines”, and larger 330 kV tower bases need wider protected areas (GNA, 4 September 2026).

We report those strips by default for 161 kV and 330 kV lines, and measure to the widths you give us for other voltages and for distribution lines.

What we map along the line

A register of what stands in the strip, then what changed

The first survey lists each structure the review confirms inside the protected strip and in the wider bands you choose, with an ID, its distance to the centre line, its band, its chainage and its coordinates. Results are grouped by 500 m segment, or by span where you send the tower positions, and each segment is rated high, medium or low by the number of structures near the line, so land-management teams can plan their visits.

Re-surveys then flag what changed: new and removed structures, fresh excavation near towers, cleared ground and new tracks across the corridor, each confirmed by a reviewer, with before-and-after views. A change notice after each scheduled survey says what changed and where. Reviewers can also tag each structure with what the imagery shows, such as main building, outbuilding, livestock enclosure or under construction.

What you receive

  • A structure register by strip, band and chainage
  • A segment or span rating along the line
  • Fresh excavation near towers flagged between surveys
  • Vegetation regrowth and burnt areas in the corridor
  • A change notice after each re-survey
  • A PDF report and GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers

What the register is for

Safety, engagement and compensation planning

Safety

Structures and digging inside a protected strip are a risk to the people using them and to the line. The register shows where that risk is concentrated, so safety work starts on the right spans.

Engagement

A dated map of what stands where gives the line owner, chiefs and traditional authorities, the District Assembly and the people along the line the same facts to talk about.

Compensation

Where compensation is due, the register records which structures stood in the strip on which imagery date. Entitlement and value are for the owner, valuers and the process the law sets out.

We map land, not people. We do not produce lists of occupants, identify anyone or take part in enforcement, and whether a structure is authorised is for the line owner and the authorities to decide.

Vegetation and bush burning

Where the corridor has regrown, and where it has burnt

We map where vegetation inside the corridor has been cleared or has regrown between dates, from Copernicus Sentinel data and very-high-resolution scenes, and where tall vegetation stands close to the conductors, from drone elevation models where flown and open canopy-height data elsewhere. The open data is older in places, so a drone survey gives the current picture, and none of it is a measured clearance to the conductors. The results come as layers your vegetation-management contractors can use to plan clearing by stretch.

Satellite-detected fire hotspots from NASA FIRMS, filtered to the buffers around the line and checked by a reviewer, are passed on as notices, and burnt areas are mapped after the fire, so the line team knows which stretches to inspect. The notices are not an emergency or early-warning service, and small, short-lived or cloud-covered fires can be missed.

New lines and upgrades

Count the structures before the route is fixed

For a new line, an interconnector or an upgrade, we compare route options side by side: the structures within set distances of each alignment, how built-up land has grown near each one, and the stretches that cross steep or flood-prone ground. Once the route is chosen, a dated register along it is the baseline for acquisition and compensation, and later re-surveys show what appeared after that date.

Customary land matters here. Stool, skin and family land is administered with chiefs, and the Office of the Administrator of Stool Lands collects ground rent, so the engagement plan for a new line starts with traditional authorities as well as the District Assembly. A shared, dated map helps both.

Route and site selection · Cut-off-date baselines in Ghana

Drones near high-tension lines

Why transmission work in Ghana starts from satellite

Drone flights near high-tension wires need a special GCAA authorisation, because Part 28 lists areas of high radio interference among the operations that need one. Flights within 30 m of buildings, vehicles or groups of people need explicit permission, and flights over congested areas need GCAA permission unless the drone can land safely in an emergency. Power stations are also on the GCAA’s list of no-fly facilities.

So the whole line is screened from satellite first, and drone checks are planned only for the spans that need more detail, subject to the GCAA authorisations and security clearances each job requires. Where your own line teams already fly drones, we run the analysis on their imagery.

How it works

From line route to reviewed register

  1. Scope

    You send the line route or tower positions, the voltage and what the register is for. We agree the widths, imagery and deliverables in a written proposal.

  2. Screen

    Dated satellite scenes and open building datasets give the first register along the whole line, with no one on site.

  3. Review

    A person checks and completes the register, and lists what the imagery cannot settle for a field check.

  4. Repeat

    Re-surveys on the schedule you set, with a change notice after each one, and drone checks of flagged spans where the approvals allow.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Map structures, excavation, cleared ground and vegetation visible from the air
  • Measure each structure to the centre line and group it along the line
  • Flag change between dated surveys, confirmed by a reviewer
  • Compare route options before a new line is built

What we don’t do

  • Identify, count or follow people, or list occupants
  • Take part in enforcement, or decide whether a structure is authorised
  • Settle ownership, entitlement or value
  • Inspect conductors, insulators or towers for defects

Frequently asked questions

Is the register a list for clearing the corridor?

No. It records which structures stand where, how far each is from the centre line and on which imagery date it first appears. It is made for safety planning, for engagement with the people, chiefs and assemblies along the line, and for compensation processes. Decisions about any structure are for the line owner, the authorities and the procedures the law sets out, not for us.

Which widths do you measure?

For 161 kV and 330 kV lines, the protected strips of 15 m and 20 m either side of the centre of the line, as GRIDCo describes the transmission-line protection regulations. For other voltages, interconnectors and distribution lines, we measure to the widths you give us. Wider bands can be added for planning, and each structure carries its exact distance.

Can you tell who trades or lives under the line?

No. We map land, not people. The register can show a kiosk, a shed, a house or a walled compound, and the date it first appears; it never shows who uses it, and it records no names.

Can a drone survey the line instead?

Only with a special authorisation, because Part 28 of the Ghana Civil Aviation Directives lists areas of high radio interference, such as high-tension wires, among the operations that need one. Flights within 30 m of buildings, vehicles or groups of people also need explicit permission. A satellite register comes first, and drone checks follow on the stretches that need them, subject to the GCAA authorisations and security clearances each job requires.

Can you show vegetation growing into the right of way?

Yes. We map where vegetation has regrown or been cleared inside the corridor between dates, and where tall vegetation stands, from drone elevation models where flown and open canopy-height data elsewhere. The open data is older in places, so a drone survey gives the current picture, and none of it is a measured clearance to a conductor. Burnt areas after bush fires are mapped from satellite data too.

Can the register support compensation claims?

It supports them with a neutral, dated record: which structures stood inside the strip on which imagery date, and which appeared later. Who is entitled to compensation, and how much, is decided by the line owner, valuers and the process the law sets out; the register does not settle ownership, use or value.

Send your line route

Send the line route or tower positions (KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile or GeoPackage), the voltage, the regions and districts it crosses and what the register is for. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
